section_title: How does rejection by the Philistine commanders release David?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Now the Philistines brought all their forces together at Aphek, while Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel. 2 As the Philistine leaders marched out with their units of hundreds and thousands, David and his men marched behind them with Achish. 3 Then the commanders of the Philistines asked, “What about these Hebrews?” Achish replied, “Is this not David, the servant of King Saul of Israel? He has been with me all these days, even years, and from the day he defected until today I have found no fault in him.” 4 But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with Achish and told him, “Send that man back and let him return to the place you assigned him. He must not go down with us into battle only to become our adversary during the war. What better way for him to regain the favor of his master than with the heads of our men? 5 Is this not the David about whom they sing in their dances: ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?”

6 So Achish summoned David and told him, “As surely as the LORD lives, you have been upright, and it seems right in my sight that you should march in and out with me in the army, because I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until this day. But you are not good in the sight of the leaders. 7 Therefore turn back now and go in peace, so that you will not do anything to displease the leaders of the Philistines.” 8 “But what have I done?” David replied. “What have you found against your servant, from the day I came to you until today, to keep me from going along to fight against the enemies of my lord the king?” 9 Achish replied, “I know that you are as pleasing in my sight as an angel of God. But the commanders of the Philistines have said, ‘He must not go into battle with us.’ 10 Now then, get up early in the morning, along with your master’s servants who came with you, and go as soon as it is light.” 11 So David and his men got up early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. And the Philistines went up to Jezreel.

context_lines: The story returns to the gathering of the Philistine forces at Aphek. David and his men march at the rear with Achish. Other commanders object to the Hebrews being among them, fearing David could regain Saul’s favor by turning against them during battle.

They remember the song celebrating David’s victories. Achish trusts him, but the other leaders do not. Achish repeatedly tells David that he has found no fault in him, then orders him to return because the commanders will not accept his presence.

David protests that he has given no cause for rejection and asks why he cannot fight the enemies of his lord the king. Achish insists. David and his men leave early for Philistine territory while the army goes up to Jezreel. He is released from a battle that would put his loyalties under severe strain.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/29.htm) see God’s care in the commanders’ refusal. Their suspicion frees David from a situation in which serving one side threatens his obligations to the other. What appears to be an unwelcome dismissal becomes a deliverance.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/29.htm) read David’s protest as a performance intended to preserve Achish’s trust. Gill thinks David is inwardly relieved. That explains the protest as continued deception, but the narrative itself does not disclose his full battle plan or every private feeling.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/29.htm) emphasizes the danger of coming close to wrongdoing through fear of people. Achish’s favorable opinion is sincere within what he knows; it does not reveal the whole truth about David’s raids or resolve the dilemma.
god_plan_lines: David’s release shows how help can come through people who are acting from their own suspicions. Their refusal prevents his involvement in the coming battle and sends him back toward the families who will need rescue.

[1 Corinthians 10:12–13](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/10.htm) joins a warning against self-confidence with assurance of God’s faithfulness in temptation. He provides a way to endure rather than requiring His people to surrender to wrongdoing. David’s unexpected release offers a human example of receiving a way out of a dangerous entanglement.

This is a parallel about God’s help, rather than a rule that every rejection is a personal message from Him or that every bad decision ends without consequences. The next chapter shows the losses David still has to face.
